paragraphs: Direct Feedback Alignment trains neural networks using random feedback weights instead of the backward signals used by backpropagation. Its success varies sharply across architectures: it can train Transformers, yet struggles with convolutional networks. This paper develops a theory aimed at explaining how this alternative learning process works and why those differences arise.

For shallow networks, the authors identify two stages. First, the weights adapt so that the approximate learning direction aligns with the true loss gradient. The network then concentrates on fitting the data. This sequence also selects among otherwise low-loss solutions: the analysis describes a preference for the solution with the strongest gradient alignment.

For deep linear networks, the conditioning of alignment matrices helps explain how data structure affects alignment and suggests an explanation for convolutional networks' difficulties. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR10 demonstrate solution selection in deep nonlinear networks, with alignment followed by memorization progressing from lower layers upward. The findings connect the feedback mechanism to both learning order and the solutions training favors.
icml-2021-align-then-memorise-the-dynami.tldr: A theory of feedback alignment describes how networks first align learning signals and then fit data, helping explain architecture-dependent training behavior.

paragraphs: Forecasting many related time series requires describing possible future values together, including their uncertainty and relationships. This paper introduces TimeGrad, an autoregressive forecasting model that generates samples at successive time steps. Its target is a distribution of outcomes across multiple variables, allowing forecasts to express more than a single predicted future.

TimeGrad uses diffusion probabilistic models to learn the gradient information needed for sampling. Training optimizes a variational bound on the likelihood of the data. At prediction time, the model starts with white noise and uses a Markov chain with Langevin sampling to transform that noise into a sample from the distribution of interest.

This connects sequential forecasting with a generative procedure that builds samples through repeated updates. The authors report state-of-the-art multivariate probabilistic forecasting results in experiments on real-world datasets containing thousands of correlated dimensions. Those results support the usefulness of the approach for the evaluated high-dimensional forecasting problems, while the proposed combination provides a direction for further research into diffusion-based time series models.
icml-2021-autoregressive-denoising-diffu.tldr: TimeGrad uses autoregressive diffusion sampling to produce probabilistic forecasts and reports state-of-the-art results on high-dimensional real-world time series.

paragraphs: Disentangled representation learning seeks to separate the underlying factors that generate observations. The paper addresses a mismatch between common approaches to this goal and the structure of many real-world processes. Existing algorithms and evaluation metrics often treat those factors, and their learned representations, as a flat collection of independent continuous variables.

The authors instead focus on settings with hierarchical organization. Such processes can combine discrete choices with continuous variation, contain dependencies between factors, and have different intrinsic dimensionalities in different parts of the hierarchy. These properties change what a faithful representation should capture: separating variables alone does not describe their organization or dependence.

The contribution is a coordinated set of benchmarks, algorithms, and metrics for learning hierarchical representations. Benchmarks provide problems with the relevant structure, algorithms address how to learn it, and metrics address how to assess the result. Together, these components broaden the study of disentanglement beyond flat factor collections and give researchers a way to investigate representations that reflect more complicated generative processes.
icml-2021-benchmarks-algorithms-and-metr.tldr: The paper develops benchmarks, algorithms, and metrics for disentangled representations with hierarchical, dependent, and mixed discrete-continuous factors.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a bandit problem in which decisions are assigned to the nodes of a graph. The learner observes a noisy reward on each edge, reflecting the interaction between the choices at its two endpoints. Rewards have a bilinear form, so the problem explicitly represents how pairs of assigned choices work together.

The objective is to identify the allocation that maximizes the sum of rewards across the graph. This makes the decision a coordinated assignment problem: the value of a choice depends on the neighboring choices with which it interacts. The authors exploit the geometry of this structure to develop a decentralized allocation strategy based on random sampling.

The strategy comes with theoretical guarantees, including a characterization of how graph structure affects its convergence rate. Star, complete, and circular graphs illustrate the kinds of topology considered. Empirical experiments confirm the reported dependence on graph structure. The contribution therefore links the efficiency of identifying a good allocation to the organization of interactions, alongside providing a sampling-based method for doing so.
icml-2021-best-arm-identification-in-gra.tldr: A decentralized random-sampling strategy identifies rewarding graph allocations, with guarantees describing how graph structure affects convergence.

paragraphs: Some neural networks, under particular initializations, have learning dynamics closely described by kernel methods. This raises a question about whether successful neural learning depends on a corresponding kernel method also succeeding. The paper investigates that question through classification of high-dimensional Gaussian mixtures, providing a setting where the two approaches behave differently.

The authors show that two-layer networks with only a few neurons can achieve near-optimal performance in this setting, while lazy training methods, including random features and kernel methods, do not. Their analysis derives ordinary differential equations that exactly track the network dynamics. These equations make it possible to determine asymptotic performance as regularization or the signal-to-noise ratio changes.

The analysis also separates the speed of learning from its final outcome. Adding more network parameters speeds convergence in the studied problem without improving the final performance. Together, these findings establish a concrete separation between neural networks and the kernel approaches considered, while showing that larger networks can offer an optimization benefit even when the eventual classification performance stays the same.
icml-2021-classifying-high-dimensional-g.tldr: In a high-dimensional Gaussian mixture problem, small two-layer networks achieve near-optimal classification where the studied kernel and random-feature methods do not.

paragraphs: Imitation learning uses expert behavior to help train agents without designing a reward function from scratch. Many methods assume that the expert and learner operate in the same environment. This paper studies transfer when their environments differ in dynamics, viewpoint, or body structure, making expert observations difficult to use directly.

The proposed framework learns a correspondence between the two domains from trajectories that are neither paired nor aligned. Expert trajectories contain states alone. To establish a correspondence, the method imposes cycle consistency in both the state space and a shared latent space. This encourages mappings across domains and back to remain consistent with the original information.

A normalized position estimator adds a temporal constraint, aligning states according to their relative positions within trajectories. Once the correspondence is learned, expert demonstrations can be transferred into the learner's domain and used for imitation. Experiments across varied challenging domains demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The main contribution is making observational demonstrations usable across domain differences through learned spatial and temporal correspondences.
icml-2021-cross-domain-imitation-from-ob.tldr: The method learns cross-domain correspondences from unpaired state trajectories so expert demonstrations can support imitation in a different environment.

paragraphs: Many learning problems rely on comparing distributions, including generative modeling and adaptation between domains. This paper puts privacy protection directly into that comparison. It focuses on making the Sliced Wasserstein Distance differentially private, providing a distribution-comparison mechanism that can become a component of larger learning algorithms.

The authors analyze adding Gaussian perturbations to the distance's existing randomized mechanism and establish the sensitivity of the resulting private mechanism. Sensitivity is central to determining how changes in the input affect what is released. A key finding is that this procedure produces another distance, which they name the Smoothed Sliced Wasserstein Distance.

That result gives the privacy mechanism a useful interpretation as a modified distribution distance that can be incorporated into generative models and domain adaptation algorithms. Experiments show highly competitive performance against gradient-based differential privacy approaches. For the domain adaptation problems considered, the authors report almost no accuracy loss. The evidence supports protecting this foundational comparison operation as a practical route to private learning in the evaluated settings.
icml-2021-differentially-private-sliced-.tldr: Adding Gaussian perturbations to Sliced Wasserstein comparisons yields a private smoothed distance with competitive empirical performance.

paragraphs: Gradient-based learning in two-player games can be difficult to stabilize because each player's updates interact with the other's. This paper studies a source of that complexity: taking discrete optimization steps changes the dynamics relative to continuous gradient flow. The authors call this difference discretization drift and examine both simultaneous and alternating updates.

Using backward error analysis, they derive modified continuous dynamical systems that closely track the discrete learning process. These systems expose effects that are obscured when analysis focuses only on the original continuous flow. The authors identify separate components of drift that can change performance and, in some cases, make a game unstable.

The analysis applies to challenges in zero-sum games, including generative adversarial networks. Quantifying the drift also points to regularizers that cancel harmful components or reinforce beneficial ones, improving GAN training performance. The contribution is both explanatory and practical: it relates training behavior to the discrete update rule and uses that relationship to design interventions targeted at particular effects of discretization.
icml-2021-discretization-drift-in-two-pl.tldr: Analyzing how discrete updates alter two-player dynamics reveals drift components that can be controlled to improve GAN training.

paragraphs: When a learning problem has many possible labels, computing a loss over all of them can be expensive. Negative sampling reduces that cost by using a subset of labels. This paper examines how that computational choice also changes learning behavior, particularly when some labels occur much more frequently than others.

The authors establish a connection between negative sampling and modifications to loss functions intended to address label imbalance. Different sampling schemes implicitly favor different balances of performance on common and rare labels. Sampling therefore affects more than the cost of approximating the loss: it can also influence which parts of the label distribution the model serves well.

The paper provides a unified way to address two sources of bias explicitly. Sampling bias comes from considering only a subset of labels, while labeling bias comes from imbalance already present in the data. Experiments on long-tail classification and retrieval benchmarks verify the findings. This distinction makes it possible to reason about computational sampling choices and data imbalance together while retaining their separate roles.
icml-2021-disentangling-sampling-and-lab.tldr: Negative sampling implicitly trades performance between common and rare labels, motivating a unified treatment of sampling bias and label imbalance.

paragraphs: Hierarchical forecasting must describe uncertainty while respecting relationships between series at different aggregation levels. Forecasts are coherent when those relationships hold together. This paper presents a model that learns probabilistic forecasts and their reconciliation in one training process, removing the need for an explicit reconciliation stage after prediction.

The model learns simultaneously from all series in the hierarchy. It expresses reconciliation as an optimization problem with a closed-form solution and uses the reparameterization trick to support end-to-end learning. These components allow the consistency-enforcing operation to participate in training, connecting what the model learns with the aggregation relationships its forecasts must satisfy.

The approach also supports broader aggregation constraints, including grouped and temporal hierarchies. Its contribution therefore extends beyond a single form of hierarchical organization. An extensive evaluation on real-world hierarchical datasets demonstrates advantages over the state of the art. The stated findings support integrating reconciliation into a trainable probabilistic model as a way to produce forecasts that express uncertainty and agree across the required aggregations.
icml-2021-end-to-end-learning-of-coheren.tldr: A single trainable model incorporates reconciliation to produce probabilistic hierarchical forecasts that satisfy aggregation constraints.

paragraphs: Neural detectors can be evaded when an attacker makes small changes to an input while preserving its purpose. This paper addresses that vulnerability for networks with binary inputs, including security detection settings. It introduces Fourier stabilization, a way to modify individual neurons so that the network becomes more robust to evasion.

The method replaces a neuron's weights with robust alternatives derived using Fourier analysis. Deciding which neurons to modify becomes a combinatorial optimization problem, and the authors propose several approximate solution methods. This makes neuron selection part of the defense design, alongside the mathematical construction of the replacement weights themselves.

The authors provide a formal bound on the accuracy drop caused by stabilizing an individual neuron. Experiments in several detection settings show improved network robustness, and the approach also combines effectively with adversarial training. The contribution joins a targeted change to neuron weights with an explicit analysis of its local accuracy cost and empirical evidence that it can complement another established form of defense.
icml-2021-enhancing-robustness-of-neural.tldr: Fourier stabilization replaces selected neurons' weights to improve evasion robustness in binary-input networks and combines effectively with adversarial training.

paragraphs: Particle-based variational inference approximates a target distribution without the arbitrary parametric assumptions common in other variational methods. However, many particle methods do not provide a way to draw arbitrary new posterior samples. This paper introduces Generative Particle Variational Inference, or GPVI, to combine particle-based inference with a learned generative sampler.

GPVI trains a neural sampler using the functional gradient of the KL divergence between its empirical sampling distribution and the target. The construction assumes that this gradient belongs to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The resulting method maintains the asymptotic performance of particle-based variational inference while providing the flexibility to generate samples through a neural model.

Experiments cover both exactly known and intractable target distributions. GPVI outperforms earlier generative particle methods, including amortized SVGD, and is competitive with particle-based inference and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. These results support the proposed combination in the tested settings: a sampler that can generate additional approximate posterior draws while retaining the distribution-fitting strengths associated with particle-based methods.
icml-2021-generative-particle-variationa.tldr: GPVI learns a neural posterior sampler using functional gradients, combining generative sampling flexibility with the asymptotic performance of particle-based inference.

paragraphs: Implicit regularization concerns the preferences a learning algorithm exhibits through its training process. This paper studies those preferences in tensor factorization, extending a theoretical line of work on matrix factorization. The tensor-completion setting corresponds to a certain type of nonlinear neural network, bringing the analysis closer to nonlinear learning.

The authors use a dynamical-systems perspective to characterize how gradient descent evolves the factorization. Their characterization suggests a greedy search toward low tensor rank. They prove this behavior under certain conditions and demonstrate it empirically under others. The distinction matters: the paper combines a conditional theoretical result with evidence beyond the conditions covered by that proof.

Motivated by this connection, the authors also investigate tensor rank as an empirical measure of complexity. They find that it captures important characteristics of datasets on which neural networks generalize. The work therefore proposes tensor rank as a promising route toward explaining training-induced preferences and their relationship to data properties, while presenting that broader explanatory role as a possibility for further development.
icml-2021-implicit-regularization-in-ten.tldr: Gradient-descent dynamics in tensor factorization suggest a greedy low-rank search, proved under certain conditions and supported empirically under others.

paragraphs: Graph matching seeks correspondences between nodes in different graphs, but adversarial input changes can cause incorrect matches. This paper identifies two topology-based attack types: inter-graph dispersion and intra-graph assembly. It introduces an integrated defense, IDRGM, with separate techniques designed to address both forms of manipulation simultaneously.

The defense against inter-graph dispersion uses geometric detection involving simplexes inscribed in hyperspheres formed from multiple matched nodes. Its construction spreads matched nodes across graphs into regular-simplex arrangements. The technique uses the geometry of a group of corresponding nodes as part of the defense against this attack type.

For intra-graph assembly, the method estimates the distribution of perturbed graphs using a phase-type distribution and maximum likelihood estimation. It then separates nodes within a graph over a wider space, significantly reducing interference from similar neighbors of perturbed nodes. The authors evaluate IDRGM's robustness on real datasets against state-of-the-art algorithms. The contribution is an integrated treatment of two distinct attack mechanisms through geometric detection and distribution-based node separation.
icml-2021-integrated-defense-for-resilie.tldr: IDRGM combines geometric detection and distribution-based node separation to defend graph matching against two topology-based attack types.

paragraphs: A feature learned inside a deep neural network can contain components with different levels of complexity. This paper develops a general definition of feature complexity and a method for examining those components separately. Its goal is to make the structure of a learned feature available for interpretation and analysis.

Given a feature from a particular network layer, the method decomposes it into components of different complexity orders and visualizes them. This decomposition supports evaluating how reliable and effective the components are, as well as how strongly they exhibit overfitting. It provides a more detailed object of study than treating the layer's feature as a single undivided representation.

The authors report that this analysis can help improve neural-network performance. They also use feature complexity to offer insights into network compression and knowledge distillation. The central contribution is a shared framework for asking what different parts of a representation contribute, connecting visualization with assessments of usefulness and overfitting rather than leaving interpretation as a purely descriptive exercise.
icml-2021-interpreting-and-disentangling.tldr: A feature-complexity framework decomposes network representations to examine component reliability, usefulness, and overfitting.

paragraphs: Answering complex questions over a knowledge graph requires connecting natural-language meaning with multiple reasoning steps. Missing graph links create a particular difficulty for methods that execute a structured query by traversing existing edges. LEGO addresses this problem by combining incremental query construction with execution in a learned latent space.

The framework alternates between two components. A Query Synthesizer proposes a reasoning action and extends the query tree one step at a time. A Latent Space Executor carries out that action using embeddings, helping the reasoning process cope with missing graph information. Query construction and execution therefore proceed together throughout the reasoning sequence.

To train the synthesizer without supervision for every intermediate step, the authors introduce a bottom-up search procedure guided by latent execution. It efficiently seeks useful execution traces within a large space of possible queries. Experiments on several knowledge-graph question-answering benchmarks demonstrate effectiveness relative to previous state-of-the-art methods. The contribution connects structured reasoning with latent execution while also providing a way to learn the reasoning sequence without stepwise labels.
icml-2021-lego-latent-execution-guided-r.tldr: LEGO alternates query synthesis with latent-space execution to answer multi-hop questions over incomplete knowledge graphs.

paragraphs: Protein language modeling has learned useful structure and function information from large collections of sequences. Earlier models described here make predictions from individual sequences, while a longstanding biological approach studies families of related sequences separately. MSA Transformer combines information from related sequences with training shared across many protein families.

The model takes a multiple sequence alignment as input, bringing a set of evolutionarily related sequences into one representation. It interleaves row and column attention across this input, allowing processing along both directions of the alignment. Training uses a variant of masked language modeling across many families, combining family-level input with broadly shared learning.

The authors report a large improvement over the current state of the art in unsupervised structure learning. They also report substantially greater parameter efficiency than earlier leading protein language models. These findings support using aligned sequence families as inputs to a shared language model: the architecture can draw on relationships within an alignment while benefiting from training across many different families.
icml-2021-msa-transformer-4cff22d703.tldr: MSA Transformer learns from aligned protein families and reports stronger unsupervised structure learning with much greater parameter efficiency.

paragraphs: Identifiability asks whether a model can be determined from data with sufficient precision and resources. Deep representation models complicate this question because their overparameterized weights do not uniquely identify their behavior. This paper shifts attention to the learned representation function and asks whether its ambiguity can be characterized more narrowly.

Building on work in nonlinear Independent Components Analysis, the authors show that a large family of discriminative models can be identifiable in function space up to a linear transformation. This means the remaining ambiguity concerns a linear change in the representation, even though the representation function itself can be nonlinear. The paper derives sufficient conditions for this form of identifiability.

The result covers many representation-learning models used for text, images, and audio, including models that were state of the art at publication. Experiments on simulated and real-world data provide empirical support. The contribution gives a precise sense in which learned representations can be determined despite ambiguity in network weights, with the guarantee tied to the stated sufficient conditions.
icml-2021-on-linear-identifiability-of-l.tldr: Under sufficient conditions, a broad family of discriminative models learns representations identifiable up to a linear transformation.

paragraphs: Pruning removes network parameters, raising the question of how much predictive performance changes as the remaining network becomes sparse. This paper finds that the error of iteratively magnitude-pruned networks empirically follows a scaling law. Its coefficients have interpretations and depend on the architecture and task, giving the relationship a structured form.

The authors approximate prediction error using an invariant that combines network width, depth, and pruning level. Within this approximation, networks with very different remaining parameter densities can be interchangeable in terms of error. This connects several design choices through one relationship instead of examining the effect of each choice separately.

The approximation is accurate across orders of magnitude in depth, width, dataset size, and density. The authors also show that its functional form generalizes to large-scale settings, including ImageNet and ResNets. These are empirical findings about the studied pruning process. They suggest a framework for reasoning about the performance consequences of unstructured pruning as network size and training cost continue to grow.
icml-2021-on-the-predictability-of-pruni.tldr: An empirical scaling law predicts magnitude-pruned network error through a relationship among width, depth, and pruning level.

paragraphs: This paper develops neural networks for data represented on simplicial complexes, with trajectory prediction as the application. It begins by specifying three properties an architecture should satisfy. These properties address arbitrary representation choices and ensure that the network uses the broader structure of the complex when producing its output.

Permutation equivariance accounts for arbitrary node indexing, while orientation equivariance accounts for arbitrary simplex orientations. Simplicial awareness requires the output to depend on the entire complex rather than only a subset of its dimensions. Together, the criteria distinguish meaningful structural information from choices made when encoding that structure for computation.

Using tools from algebraic topology, the authors propose a simple convolutional architecture and show that it satisfies all three properties when it uses an odd nonlinear activation function. Experiments demonstrate effective trajectory extrapolation on synthetic and real datasets, particularly improved generalization to unseen trajectories. The contribution links explicit architectural principles to a concrete model and supports their usefulness through the reported prediction results.
icml-2021-principled-simplicial-neural-n.tldr: A simplicial convolutional architecture satisfies three structural principles under an odd nonlinear activation and improves generalization to unseen trajectories.

paragraphs: Calls for more representative training data often aim to reduce performance differences between subpopulations. This paper asks how dataset composition actually shapes learning outcomes. It treats data collection as part of the learning process, making the allocation of training examples across groups an explicit subject of analysis and design.

The authors show that diverse representation matters for subgroup performance and for objectives measured across the population. Their analysis and experiments describe how changing the composition of a dataset influences performance. This connects decisions about whose examples are collected with the goals used to assess the resulting predictor.

The paper also provides constructive results for guiding dataset design using trends visible in existing data together with domain knowledge. The intended allocation is therefore informed by the learning objective and available evidence about performance. Its contribution is a framework for intentional data collection: subgroup representation becomes a decision linked to desired outcomes, helping make a broad call for diversity more concrete and operational.
icml-2021-representation-matters-assessi.tldr: Treating subgroup allocation as part of learning helps connect representative data collection with subgroup and population-level performance objectives.

paragraphs: Sharf estimates a neural scene representation of an object from one image. Its central idea is to infer an explicit geometric scaffold and use that shape to guide reconstruction of the object's radiance field. This gives the reconstruction process a geometric structure around which to organize the object's rendered appearance.

The generative process first maps one latent code into a voxelized shape, then renders an image with appearance controlled by a second latent code. For a new test image, inference optimizes both latent codes and the networks to fit that image. Separating shape from appearance enables the model to be fine-tuned using only the single observed view.

The authors report that the fitted representation supports geometrically consistent novel views that faithfully represent the input object. They also demonstrate generalization beyond the training domain, including more realistic renderings and real photographs, and find that the scaffold accurately estimates three-dimensional shape. Experiments on synthetic and real images support the combined use of explicit shape guidance and a separately controlled appearance representation.
icml-2021-sharf-shape-conditioned-radian.tldr: Sharf separates shape and appearance to reconstruct an object from one image and render geometrically consistent new views.

paragraphs: High-dimensional partial differential equations appear throughout science, engineering, and economics, but traditional grid methods face rapidly growing computational demands as dimension increases. This paper explores tensor trains as an approximation framework for parabolic equations. The approach aims to make use of latent low-rank structure for compact representation and efficient computation.

The method combines a reformulation using backward stochastic differential equations with regression in tensor format. This connects the equation-solving task to a structured approximation procedure. Within that framework, the authors develop iterative schemes with either explicit updates emphasizing speed or implicit updates emphasizing accuracy, providing different ways to balance the numerical work.

Experiments on a number of examples show a favorable balance between accuracy and computational efficiency compared with state-of-the-art neural-network-based approaches. The results support tensor trains as an appealing option for the evaluated problems. The broader motivation is that exploitable low-rank structure may reduce the burden of high dimensionality, linking compression of the approximate solution with the efficiency of the computations used to obtain it.
icml-2021-solving-high-dimensional-parab.tldr: Tensor-train regression schemes show a favorable accuracy-efficiency tradeoff for high-dimensional parabolic PDEs in the evaluated examples.

paragraphs: Automatic curriculum learning uses a teacher algorithm to select tasks as a reinforcement-learning agent's abilities change. Comparing such teachers is difficult when studies use different experimental setups. TeachMyAgent addresses this problem by providing a benchmark organized around key challenges in curriculum learning and using procedurally generated tasks.

The benchmark includes focused tests built from variants of a procedural Box2D bipedal walker environment. It also introduces a procedural Parkour environment that combines most of the identified challenges for broader assessment. This organization allows evaluation of particular difficulties alongside evaluation in a setting where several difficulties occur together.

The authors compare representative curriculum methods and find that some approaches without expert knowledge are competitive. They also report that Parkour remains an open problem, preserving a demanding target for future methods. The released Python package includes the environments, studied curriculum algorithms, and reinforcement-learning students. The contribution is a common experimental foundation for studying task selection, with initial comparisons showing both competitive existing approaches and a substantial remaining challenge.
icml-2021-teachmyagent-a-benchmark-for-a.tldr: TeachMyAgent benchmarks curriculum-learning algorithms with focused procedural tests and a challenging Parkour environment that remains an open problem.

paragraphs: Text-to-image generation connects a written description with a corresponding image. The paper examines a simple modeling approach in a field where progress had often centered on specialized architectures, additional training losses, or extra annotations such as object-part labels and segmentation masks. It shifts attention toward a shared representation of text and images.

The proposed transformer treats text tokens and image tokens as one stream. It models that stream autoregressively, predicting successive tokens from preceding ones. This places the relationship between language and visual content inside a single sequential modeling task, making the joint token stream the central organizing choice of the approach.

The authors report that, with sufficient training data and scale, this approach is competitive with earlier domain-specific models under zero-shot evaluation. The condition on data and scale is part of the finding. The result supports the idea that a comparatively simple joint modeling formulation can achieve competitive text-to-image performance when developed at sufficient scale, broadening the set of approaches available for the task.
icml-2021-zero-shot-text-to-image-genera.tldr: With sufficient data and scale, a transformer modeling text and image tokens together achieves competitive zero-shot text-to-image generation.
